desc:
You get two integer arrays nums1 and nums2 of equal length n and an integer diff. Count the pairs of indices i < j that satisfy

nums1[i] - nums1[j] ≤ nums2[i] - nums2[j] + diff.

nums1 = [5, 1, 4], nums2 = [2, 3, 0], diff = 0
rewritten per index: 3, -2, 4 -> pairs (0,2) and (1,2) qualify  -> 2
hints: Checking all pairs is O(n<sup>2</sup>). Try to rewrite the inequality so that everything about index i is on one side and everything about index j on the other.
Let d[k] = nums1[k] - nums2[k]. The condition becomes d[i] ≤ d[j] + diff for i < j. This is an inversion-style count with a shifted comparison.

Run merge sort on d. When both halves are sorted, for every right value r count the left values ≤ r + diff with a pointer that only moves forward, add that to the total, then merge. A Fenwick tree over compressed values also works.
editorial: Moving the terms around gives (nums1[i] - nums2[i]) - (nums1[j] - nums2[j]) ≤ diff, i.e. d[i] - d[j] ≤ diff with d[k] = nums1[k] - nums2[k]. So the two arrays collapse into one and we must count pairs i < j with d[i] ≤ d[j] + diff.

This is the same divide and conquer as counting inversions. Split the array, recurse, and count the crossing pairs (i in the left half, j in the right half). With both halves sorted, as d[j] grows over the sorted right half the threshold d[j] + diff grows, so the number of left values at or below it only grows. One forward-moving pointer yields all counts in linear time. Then merge and return. Counting before merging is what lets the comparison differ from the sort order.
Each level is linear and there are log n levels: O(n log n) time, O(n) memory. Note that diff may be negative, which the same code handles.
